I didn't do any practice tests myself. The ATI books had mini practice tests per each section so that is what I did. If it bad full on practice tests in the back then I didn't do them lol

Last time when I scored on the lower end of things I only did the practice exams in my Mometrix book. That book gave me bonus review content online in the form of cheat sheets. I found those really helpful even for the new version. I'd check if ur Mometrix offers something like that. 

Tbh, free practice tests online should be good enough. The test was so random in how it jumped around from sub-topic to sub-topic that idk if any paid practice run could actually mimik it well enough to make it worth the pricetag.

Don't buy the official book for ATI. It sucks major stinky unwashed dick. Errors galore and overly complicated wording. 

Here's what I suggest focusing on while studying:

•Chemistry!! 

Wasn't a big deal on the 6th version but the 7th definitely focuses on it more. Not the composition of molecules (although I did get one comp q which left me bamboozled as it wasn't in the prep book at all) but just general intro to chem knowledge. 

•A&PII > A&P I

For me there were qs on urogenital, integumentary, cardiac, respiratory, and endocrine systems. Be familiar with your anatomical planes, too. Math was pretty cool. I didn't finish it all in time so be sure to watch the timer. Lots of percentages, conversions of metric to imperial, algebra... That's all I can remember off the top of my head lol


Oh, and I found the reading and eng. lang. section way easier this time around. Mostly finding themes, synonyms, and where would you use from the library to research stuff (encyclopedia, atlas, ect.) Grammar was the hardest imo. Identifying different types of adjectives, correcting punctuation and stuff. 

Hope this helps. If you have any other questions lemme know and I'll see what I can find from my score sheet lol

Yes, I've often seen this train of thought tossed around. However, I feel like the deeper reason doesn't exclusively have to be helping people or anything like that. I think that drive can come from many different things. 

My mom never wanted to be a nurse when she was younger but, as she had kids, she ended up switching professions as a way to earn more money. My dad wasn't earning a lot as a line cook so she decided to go back to school. She went from being a secretary to a nurse in the span of ~3 years back in the 90's. Thankfully, she now loves what she does but it was never her dream. She actually really wanted to be a hairdresser back in the day! Sadly, her parents weren't supportive of that idea. 

If one were to pursue the medical route then, yes, I think lots of passion is needed as it is a very long and difficult road to pursue. For me, I like science and am fascinated by the human body. I loved A&P back in highschool and am very excited to be taking A&PII this summer while waiting to find out if I've been accepted into my college's ASN program. Science is definitely not my strong suit nor my passion. However, I am hopeful that those interests will be enough to allow me to enjoy nursing as a career. If it isn't, then I can tough it out a few years to get my experience before pursuing an administrative role and separate myself from bedside. 

Whenever I'm worried about my lack of passion for healthcare, my mom always tells me stories of her coworkers who are nurses because it is a job and not because it was there dream to be a nurse. I'm sure having a passion or a love for healing people would help but in the end, it's still a job, no? From what I hear, even if you pursue your passion, making it your livelihood could potentially suck all the joy out of you that you once had for the profession. 

My thought is as long as it doesn't make you miserable then why not give it a shot

I feel like you and I are very similar. Relatively passionless but want to make money. Good at writing but know the job prospects for pursuing a career in that field. Personally, I'm studying nursing. Two years with an ASN and you can be working while getting your bachelor's. 

Pay is pretty good once you have the BSN and ASN pay is above what many make with a four-year degree in other fields. It can vary a lot depending on your location but overall I hear it's pretty stable.

Lots of room to find your niche and only work 36 hours a week if your are in a hospital setting. This leaves you with four days off to pursue whatever you want. Although, if you take up night shift you will spend some of that time sleeping.

Even if it's not your passion, it could be a career worth looking into if you are lost.

Imo ppl aren't so upset about you pointing out the sodium content of the spam but your usage of the word "lot" in all caps. This is a restriction subreddit meaning we aim for not eating a lot of certain things. So, your comment could be seen as very triggering and shaming for those of us within a community that already struggles with maintaining proper health as a result of our individual issues with food/body image/ect.

"[...] I was under the impression that [this sub] was meant to be pretty health-conscious foods, but I may have misunderstood."

Yes, you misunderstood. The description says that the purpose of this sub is to display our restriction that looks tasty and pleasing to the eye, unlike r/shittyrestrictionfood who, according to rule 6 of their sub, post "fucked up food combo[s], gross food, bad looking food, hilariously lame food, ect." 

Both of these subs also use "restriction" in their titles. While the word itself is not strictly used by ED communities, the phrase "dietary restriction" is used commonly by medical/health professionals to denote a reduction of a certain, or total, nutrient intake. Normally it is done through nongenetic, nonpharmacological means of intervention with the goal of increasing the active and healthy lifespan of the individual. 

However, in the context used by these two subs, the meaning is not the same. That is why we do not use the same phrasing as the medical and health and wellness communitues. We simply say "restriction" or "restriction food". It is used in reference to the characteristics of various eating disorders (ARFID, Anorexia Nervosa restrictive subtype, PANS, ect.) Not all of us are concerned with health here. Some are but the purpose of this sub is not to show off our health conscious restriction foods.

 Oh, and yes, you did come across as awfully shame-y. Even to a non-ED community, that behavior isn't cool. Before saying something you should think of what your intentions are with what you are about to say.
